name: DEXA body fat scan

angle.text: Users get a DEXA scan to see body fat and lean mass by region, then use the number to decide whether to cut or bulk for a leaner look. It is a medical imaging method chiefly studied for bone density; its use as a physique-tracking reference comes from forum practice.

summary: A low-dose X-ray scan that splits the body into fat, lean and bone, and the reference most forum members use to check their body fat number.
note: Results vary with hydration, machine make and positioning, so readings from different scanners are not directly comparable.
currentQuick:
A DEXA (or DXA) scan uses two X-ray beams of different energies to estimate how much of the body is bone, fat and lean soft tissue. It was developed mainly to measure bone density and diagnose osteoporosis, but the same scan can report whole-body and regional body composition.
In looksmaxxing communities it is treated as a measuring tool rather than a treatment: members cite DEXA readings to establish how lean they actually are before discussing facial-fat reduction or other body-contouring options.
How it works: Tissues absorb the two X-ray energies differently. Software subtracts the bone signal and, for pixels without bone, calculates the relative fractions of fat and lean soft tissue. Wikipedia describes its accuracy as comparable to hydrostatic weighing and strongly correlated with MRI and CT.
Risks and caveats: Radiation exposure from modern machines is very low (Wikipedia gives figures as low as about 0.001 mSv). Known limitations include dependence of lean-mass readings on hydration, size and weight limits of the table, roughly 40 percent of pixels that cannot be classified because soft tissue overlaps bone, and differences between manufacturers' scanners.
deepLead:
Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DEXA or DXA) is an imaging test that passes X-rays at two energy levels through the body and uses the difference in absorption to separate bone from soft tissue. It is the most widely used technology for measuring bone mineral density and is chiefly used to diagnose and monitor osteopenia and osteoporosis . The same scan can also report whole-body and regional fat mass and lean mass, which is the use that appears in looksmaxxing discussions.
For body composition, pixels that contain no bone are treated as a mixture of fat and lean soft tissue and their proportions are calculated. Wikipedia describes the accuracy as comparable to hydrostatic weighing, with strong correlation to MRI and CT, while listing limitations: lean mass is affected by hydration, patients above certain size limits cannot be scanned, and about 40 percent of pixels cannot be measured because soft tissue overlaps bone .
In forum discussions the scan is mentioned as a way to verify a body-fat percentage before considering fat-reduction procedures. One looksmax.org reply, for example, advises confirming a sub-10 percent body-fat figure with a DEXA before consulting a clinic about ultrasound cavitation.

name: Gastric bypass (Roux-en-Y)

angle.text: Discussed in hardmaxx circles as the most powerful route to large weight loss and the leaner body and face that follow. It is studied extensively for severe obesity; its use for cosmetic leaning is not what the research addresses.

summary: Major bariatric surgery that reroutes the gut for large, sustained weight loss, aimed at medical obesity rather than cosmetic leaning.
note: Major abdominal surgery with lifelong nutritional follow-up; guideline eligibility is based on BMI and health conditions, not appearance.
currentQuick:
Roux-en-Y gastric bypass divides the stomach into a small upper pouch and a large remnant, then reconnects the small intestine in a Y shape so food bypasses most of the stomach and the first part of the small intestine. It is one of the most studied bariatric operations.
It appears in looksmaxxing-adjacent discussion as a hardmaxx option for weight and facial leanness, but clinical guidance frames it as a treatment for severe obesity and obesity-related disease.
How it works: It was traditionally explained as restriction plus malabsorption. More recent work points to changes in gut hormones (reduced ghrelin; altered CCK, PYY, GLP-1), eating behavior and energy expenditure, though the mechanisms remain debated [1][2].
Risks and caveats: Complications reported include anastomotic leak, ulcers, strictures, dumping syndrome, bowel obstruction and internal hernia, blood clots, and nutritional deficiencies (iron, calcium, B12, thiamine and others). Eligibility under the 1991 NIH criteria is BMI of 40 or more, or 35 or more with comorbidities.
deepLead:
Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (RYGB) is a bariatric operation in which the stomach is divided into a small upper pouch, typically about 15 to 30 mL, and a larger remnant; the small intestine is then rearranged into a Y so that food bypasses most of the stomach and the duodenum . It is performed for severe obesity and its complications, and it is one of the best-studied weight-loss operations.
Large series report loss of roughly 65 to 80 percent of excess body weight, and Wikipedia reports improvement or resolution of type 2 diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, sleep apnea and reflux in many patients . A meta-analysis of the literature published in JAMA in 2004 examined weight loss, operative mortality and four comorbidities , and the Swedish Obese Subjects study reported lower overall mortality in the surgery group than in controls .
Clinical eligibility is set by weight and health status, not by appearance. In the looksmaxxing context the procedure is sometimes listed among hardmaxx options for dramatic weight change, which is a different use from the medical indication.

name: Gastric balloon / endoscopic sleeve

angle.text: Users look at these non-surgical devices as a way to lose a moderate amount of weight without an operation, for a leaner body and face. Trials measure weight loss in people with obesity; cosmetic outcomes are not the studied endpoint.

summary: Non-surgical stomach-reduction devices and stitching procedures that produce modest to moderate weight loss, with real procedural risks.
note: Balloons are temporary; weight is commonly regained without lifestyle change, and FDA has issued safety communications on liquid-filled balloons.
currentQuick:
An intragastric balloon is a deflated silicone balloon placed in the stomach, usually endoscopically, and filled to take up space and encourage fullness. It stays for months and is then removed. Endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty (ESG) is a separate procedure in which the stomach is sutured into a narrower tube without incisions.
Both are positioned between lifestyle change and surgery for people with obesity. They appear in hardmaxx discussions as a way to lose weight without a major operation.
How it works: A balloon occupies stomach volume and slows emptying, which promotes early fullness. Research on gastric distension has shown that stretching the stomach activates satiety circuits in the brain and reduces food intake in lean and obese people. ESG uses sutures to reshape the stomach into a narrower tube.
Risks and caveats: Common effects are nausea, vomiting, cramps and reflux. Rarer problems include ulcer, perforation and obstruction after deflation or migration. The 2022 MERIT trial of ESG reported rare serious events such as bleeding and leak. Weight regain after balloon removal is common without behavior change.
deepLead:
An intragastric balloon (gastric balloon) is an inflatable device placed in the stomach to help with weight loss when diet and exercise have not worked and surgery is not wanted or recommended. It takes up space in the stomach, which causes earlier fullness and slower gastric emptying . Devices are usually filled with saline, and some contain a dye that colors urine if the balloon leaks .
Endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty (ESG) is a different, incisionless procedure in which a physician sutures the stomach into a narrower tube using an endoscopic suturing device. In July 2022 the US FDA authorized ESG with the Apollo Overstitch device for adults with BMI 30 to 50 .
Reported results are moderate: balloon studies cited by Wikipedia report roughly 11 to 14 percent total body weight loss for one swallowable balloon, depending on follow-up, and a 2022 randomized trial of ESG reported 13.6 percent total body weight loss at one year . The procedures are marketed to people with obesity; in looksmaxxing forums they are mentioned as hardmaxx options, but the published research concerns medical obesity, not cosmetic outcomes.

name: CoolSculpting (cryolipolysis)

chain: Local fat layer thins over weeks
angle.text: Promoted for thinning stubborn local fat, including under the chin and along the jawline, for a sharper contour. Studies show modest local reductions in cleared body areas; claims about brown-fat conversion and facial use are forum theories.

summary: Controlled cold applied to a patch of fat to reduce it without surgery; studies show modest local reductions and a rare paradoxical-growth risk.
note: Reduction is modest and localized, not weight loss; rare paradoxical adipose hyperplasia (about 0.12 to 1.0 percent in reports) can require surgery to correct.
currentQuick:
Cryolipolysis cools a section of subcutaneous fat with an applicator to a temperature intended to injure fat cells while sparing skin. The body then clears the damaged cells over the following weeks. CoolSculpting is the best-known brand.
Systematic reviews report modest reductions in fat-layer thickness in treated areas, with high satisfaction. Forum members have discussed it as a way to reduce local fat, including the chin and cheeks.
How it works: Fat cells are more sensitive to cold than the overlying skin. Controlled cooling is thought to trigger apoptosis-like fat-cell injury and gradual removal by the body, shown in pig experiments published in 2009.
Risks and caveats: Common effects are redness, numbness, swelling, bruising and mild pain, usually resolving within weeks. Paradoxical adipose hyperplasia, in which treated fat enlarges, has been reported at roughly 0.12 to 1.0 percent and can require liposuction or abdominoplasty to treat.
deepLead:
Cryolipolysis, often called fat freezing, is a non-invasive procedure that uses controlled cooling of subcutaneous fat for localized fat reduction. The term is frequently used interchangeably with the brand name CoolSculpting, introduced in the United States in 2010 by Zeltiq Aesthetics and acquired by Allergan Aesthetics in 2017 . The FDA has cleared it for several body areas including the submental area, jawline, arms, flanks, abdomen and thighs .
Systematic reviews have reported moderate effectiveness. A 2015 review of 19 studies found skinfold thickness reductions of 10.3 to 28.5 percent with high patient satisfaction, and a 2023 review of 18 studies reported ultrasound-measured fat reductions of 2.0 to 5.1 mm and judged the treatment safe but modestly effective, with low-quality data . Reviews in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery and elsewhere address efficacy, methods and complications .
On looksmax.org the procedure has been described as a way to cause local fat loss, including a thread proposing it for facial fat pockets .

name: Ultrasound cavitation / body contouring

angle.text: Some forum members use home ultrasound devices hoping to spot-reduce face and body fat for a leaner contour. The appearance results are based on anecdote and marketing; the sources show no published cosmetic outcomes.

summary: Low-frequency ultrasound devices marketed for fat reduction, used at home by some forum members; no published results in the sources show cosmetic outcomes.
note: Forum posts themselves list burns, skin damage and asymmetry as risks; no controlled study of home facial cavitation was found.
currentQuick:
Ultrasonic cavitation for body contouring uses low-frequency ultrasound intended to create tiny bubbles in subcutaneous fat, which are said to rupture fat cells so the body can clear the contents. Clinics offer it, and consumer devices are discussed on looksmax.org for face and body fat.
The sources reviewed contain no controlled trial of home or facial cavitation for appearance. Registered studies exist of cavitation in central obesity and polycystic ovary syndrome, but results are not given here.
How it works: Cavitation in physics means the formation and violent collapse of vapor bubbles in a liquid when local pressure drops. Proponents apply this idea to fat tissue; forum guides say ultrasound makes bubbles that disrupt fat-cell membranes, after which the fat drains via the lymphatic system.
Risks and caveats: One forum guide lists deafness, blindness, skin damage, asymmetry, burns and thyroid damage as risks of the practice. No regulatory or clinical safety data on home devices appear in the sources.
deepLead:
Ultrasonic cavitation, as used in cosmetic body contouring, refers to devices that deliver low-frequency ultrasound to the skin with the aim of reducing localized subcutaneous fat. In physics, cavitation is the formation and collapse of vapor-filled bubbles in a liquid when the local pressure falls below the liquid's vapor pressure, and it can produce shock waves and high local temperatures . Cosmetic proponents apply the term to ultrasound-induced bubbles in fatty tissue.
On looksmax.org, users have posted long guides on using cavitation devices at home to reduce facial and body fat, along with threads comparing devices and discussing results . Posters describe it as spot reduction and some call it a non-invasive route to destroying fat cells, while others recommend professional treatment .
The sources reviewed contain no clinical study of cavitation for cosmetic fat reduction. Registered trials exist on cavitation in central obesity, polycystic ovary syndrome and lipedema , but their results are not described here.

name: EMSculpt muscle stimulation

chain: More muscle tone in treated area
angle.text: Clinic users book it to tone the abdomen and buttocks, with the Neo version adding heat to reduce fat for a more defined midsection. It is FDA-cleared for tone and fat reduction, and the supporting studies are mostly small clinical reviews.

summary: A clinic device that triggers intense muscle contractions with focused electromagnetic energy to tone muscle and, with the Neo version, add heat to reduce fat.
note: Published studies are small and many are industry-linked; systematic reviews describe the evidence as limited.
currentQuick:
EMSCULPT, made by BTL Industries, uses high-intensity focused electromagnetic (HIFEM) energy to cause supramaximal muscle contractions in the abdomen, buttocks and other areas. The aim is to increase muscle tone or mass. EMSCULPT NEO adds radiofrequency heating to also reduce fat.
Published studies include MRI and multi-center buttock studies, and systematic reviews that assess efficacy and safety of electromagnetic treatments for body contouring.
How it works: A magnetic field induces involuntary muscle contractions stronger than voluntary ones. The manufacturer and researchers report that this can thicken muscle and, in the NEO version, add radiofrequency heat to reduce fat.
Risks and caveats: The reviewed literature describes few adverse effects, but evidence is limited and the early studies are small. The EMSCULPT NEO device is described as FDA-cleared for muscle toning and fat reduction in a 2024 systematic review.
deepLead:
EMSCULPT (BTL Industries) is a non-invasive body-contouring treatment that uses high-intensity focused electromagnetic (HIFEM) energy to stimulate muscle contractions in areas such as the abdomen and buttocks. A 2024 systematic review describes EMSCULPT NEO as an FDA-cleared treatment for increasing muscle tone and reducing fat, in which HIFEM builds muscle mass and combined radiofrequency is intended to reduce fat .
Early studies include a 22-patient abdominal study evaluated with MRI that introduced HIFEM and established hypotheses for future research  and a multi-center study of 75 patients examining toning and lifting of gluteal muscles . Systematic reviews of electromagnetic treatments for body contouring have since been published .

name: Lipodissolve (phosphatidylcholine injections)

angle.text: People pursue these injections to dissolve small pockets of fat such as under the chin without surgery. Evidence for that use is small uncontrolled reports, and no approved product exists for it.

summary: Unapproved fat-dissolving injections of phosphatidylcholine and deoxycholate; small uncontrolled reports of fat reduction, no approved product, and documented infections and inflammation.
note: Not an FDA-approved fat-reduction product; case reports describe infections and severe inflammation after injections.
currentQuick:
Lipodissolve, also called injection lipolysis, is a cosmetic procedure in which a mixture of phosphatidylcholine and the detergent sodium deoxycholate is injected into small pockets of fat. Practitioners who offer it say it shrinks localized fat and tightens skin, and it was marketed in the 2000s as a non-surgical alternative to liposuction.
Published support consists mostly of practitioner-authored reports and small studies. Reviews describe it as having drawn scrutiny from the media and the US Food and Drug Administration. A different deoxycholic-acid-only product, Kybella, was later approved by the FDA for fat under the chin, but that approval does not cover phosphatidylcholine mixtures.
How it works: Proponents proposed that phosphatidylcholine breaks down fat, while later reviews suggest the deoxycholate detergent action, which destroys fat cell membranes, may account for observed effects. The body then clears the released material over weeks.
Risks and caveats: Reported problems include pain, bruising, swelling, nodules, severe inflammation and infection, including a published case of mycobacterial infection after injections. Mixtures are often compounded rather than manufactured to an approved standard. The FDA has not approved phosphatidylcholine injections for fat reduction.
deepLead:
Lipodissolve, also known as injection lipolysis or PC/DC injection, is a cosmetic procedure in which a mixture of phosphatidylcholine (PC) and sodium deoxycholate (DC) is injected into subcutaneous fat with the aim of reducing small localized deposits. It belongs to the broader family of mesotherapy techniques, in which substances are injected into or just beneath the skin.
Practitioners who developed the technique reported that it reduces localized fat and causes some skin retraction, and described it as an adjunct to or alternative to liposuction for patients seeking a minimally invasive option. Reviews published in the late 2000s and early 2010s described the approach as having been received with initial enthusiasm and then critical scrutiny from the media and the US Food and Drug Administration. The mesotherapy literature more broadly has been described by Wikipedia's summary of it as having limited scientific backing.
Published human evidence consists mainly of practitioner case series and small studies, and at least one registered trial was terminated early. The FDA approved a purified deoxycholic acid product, Kybella, for fat beneath the chin in 2015, which is a distinct product from phosphatidylcholine mixtures.

name: Body fat calipers

angle.text: Lifters use skinfold calipers to track body fat at home and see whether a cut or bulk is changing their physique. The method is long established in sports science, and users mostly value it for tracking changes rather than absolute numbers.

summary: Pinch-style skinfold calipers estimate body fat from fold thickness; cheap and good for tracking your own changes, less reliable as an absolute percentage.
note: Measures subcutaneous fat only; results depend on technique and chosen formula.
currentQuick:
Skinfold calipers are hand-held tools that measure the thickness of a pinched fold of skin and fat at set body sites. The readings are entered into a formula, such as Durnin-Womersley or Jackson-Pollock, to estimate body density and then body fat percentage.
In lean-gaining and cutting circles they are used to track progress without scales or scans. Sources describe them as most useful for following change over time when the same person uses the same technique, rather than as a precise absolute number.
How it works: The caliper applies a standard pressure to a pinched fold at chosen sites. Subcutaneous fat thickness is converted into an estimate of total body fat using population-based equations, with a second equation such as Siri or Brozek turning body density into a percentage.
Risks and caveats: No physical risk, but accuracy depends on site placement, pressure, caliper type and the equation used. It captures only fat under the skin and not visceral fat, and two people with similar readings can differ in total body fat.
deepLead:
Body fat calipers, also called skinfold calipers or plicometers, are hand-held instruments that measure the thickness of a pinched fold of skin and the fat beneath it at standardized body sites. The readings are used in equations that estimate whole-body fat percentage. The method is also known as the pinch test.
Reference methods such as the Durnin-Womersley and Jackson-Pollock formulas estimate body density from skinfold sums, and a second formula such as Siri or Brozek converts density to body fat percentage, which compounds the statistical error. Accuracy depends on precise site placement and consistent pressure, and sources describe the method as better for tracking change within one person than for giving a true absolute figure.
Validation studies have compared skinfold calipers with ultrasound and computed tomography for subcutaneous fat measurement, and a 1979 study examined how compressible skinfolds are, one reason caliper readings vary.

name: Body wraps

chain: Slimmer measurements for a short time
angle.text: Wraps and sauna suits are used for a quickly slimmer-looking waist or a lower tape measurement before an event. The inch loss is visible right away and, per the FDA, is water that returns; fat loss from wraps is not shown.

summary: Spa wraps and sauna suits marketed for slimming; the temporary inch loss is water, per the FDA.
note: FDA warns that rapid fluid loss can cause dehydration and electrolyte imbalance.
currentQuick:
Body wraps are spa or home treatments in which the torso or limbs are wrapped in bandages, plastic or neoprene, sometimes after mud or lotion is applied, to produce sweating. Proponents say they slim and tone the body, firm skin and remove toxins.
No clinical studies supporting those claims are cited in reference sources. The US Food and Drug Administration has said that any weight lost is fluid that is quickly replaced.
How it works: Wrapping and heat cause sweating and temporary water loss and may compress tissue, which can reduce measurements for a short time. The FDA states wraps do not dissolve fat.
Risks and caveats: The FDA warns that rapid, excessive fluid loss can cause severe dehydration and electrolyte disruption. Heat and restriction from tight wraps are additional considerations.
deepLead:
Body wraps are cosmetic or spa treatments in which part of the body is wrapped in bandages, plastic film or neoprene, often after application of mud, herbal preparations or lotions, and sometimes combined with a PVC sauna suit. Wikipedia's article on mud wraps notes that body wraps redirect to it.
Proponents claim the treatment can slim and tone the body, hydrate or firm skin, relax muscles and flush toxins through sweat. The article cites no clinical studies supporting those claims. The US FDA has stated that wraps cause temporary water loss rather than fat loss, that the fluid is quickly replaced, and that rapid excessive fluid loss can cause severe dehydration and electrolyte disturbance.

name: Peg-MGF (mechano growth factor)

angle.text: Sold as a research chemical that bodybuilders inject after training to add muscle. The appearance claim rests on theory and animal or cell work, with no human evidence, and the compound is WADA-banned.

summary: A pegylated synthetic version of the IGF-1Ec peptide sold as a research chemical for muscle growth; human evidence is absent and it is WADA-banned.
note: Not approved for any use; WADA-prohibited; research raises carcinogenicity questions.
currentQuick:
Mechano growth factor (MGF, or IGF-1Ec) is a 24-amino-acid peptide the body produces by splicing of the IGF-1 gene during muscle repair after exercise. Peg-MGF is a synthetic, pegylated version sold online as a research chemical and used by some bodybuilders for muscle gain.
The published evidence is laboratory and animal work. Reference sources report no human clinical trial results for MGF as a muscle-building drug.
How it works: Natural MGF is described as acting in muscle repair and is rapidly degraded in the body. Pegylation and amino-acid substitutions in synthetic versions are intended to improve stability.
Risks and caveats: Not approved as a medicine anywhere. The World Anti-Doping Agency prohibits MGF. A 2020 review raised concerns about potential carcinogenicity, and human safety data are not available.
deepLead:
Mechano growth factor (MGF), also called IGF-1Ec, is a naturally occurring 24-amino-acid peptide produced from the IGF-1 gene during muscle repair after exercise, and is described as having anabolic effects. PEG-MGF is a pegylated synthetic form sold as a research chemical.
Research on MGF is mainly laboratory and animal work covering muscle repair and aging, signaling in muscle growth, neuroprotection and cardiac protection, and reviews have questioned its role in repair. No human clinical trial results are reported in the reference article, which also notes the World Anti-Doping Agency has banned MGF and that a 2020 review raised concerns about potential carcinogenicity.

name: Insulin (bodybuilding use)

angle.text: Some bodybuilders use prescription insulin as an anabolic aid, believing it pushes glucose and amino acids into muscle for fuller muscle bellies. This is off-label use of a diabetes drug, and evidence of benefit in healthy lifters is thin.

summary: Prescription diabetes hormone injected by some bodybuilders for muscle fullness; evidence for benefit is thin and hypoglycemia has been linked to deaths.
note: Risk of severe hypoglycemia, coma and death; prohibited for non-diabetic athletes.
currentQuick:
Insulin is the body's main anabolic hormone and a prescription medicine for diabetes. Some bodybuilders have reportedly injected it, often alongside steroids and growth hormone, hoping for more protein synthesis, glycogen storage and fuller muscles.
A reference article states the evidence supports these effects only in a small group of drug-naive individuals, and that whether insulin improves performance is unclear.
How it works: Insulin promotes glucose uptake in muscle and fat, glycogen storage, amino-acid uptake and protein synthesis, and slows protein and fat breakdown.
Risks and caveats: The main risk is hypoglycemia, which can progress to seizures, coma, brain damage or death. Insulin misuse has been mentioned as a possible factor in bodybuilder deaths. It is prescription-only in many countries and banned for non-diabetic athletes.
deepLead:
Insulin is a peptide hormone that regulates blood glucose and is the main anabolic hormone of the body: it helps muscle and fat take in glucose, increases amino-acid uptake and protein synthesis, and slows liver glucose production and breakdown of fat and protein. As a medicine it is used for diabetes.
Some bodybuilders have reportedly injected regular insulin, often alongside anabolic steroids and growth hormone, in the belief that it increases protein synthesis, muscle glycogen storage, strength and stamina. The reference article states these effects are supported only in a small group of drug-naive individuals and notes that insulin misuse has been linked to some bodybuilder deaths.

name: Prohormones (1-Andro, 4-AD)

angle.text: Once sold as over-the-counter testosterone boosters, prohormones were taken to build muscle and strength. Studies found little muscle benefit, and androstenedione was banned in the US in 2004.

summary: Steroid precursors once sold as supplements; androstenedione was banned in the US in 2004 and studies found little muscle benefit.
note: Androstenedione is a controlled substance in the US since 2005 and banned by sports bodies.
currentQuick:
Prohormones are compounds that the body can convert into active hormones. In the 1990s, androstenedione (4-AD, called andro) was sold over the counter as a supplement for raising testosterone and building muscle, and gained fame through baseball players.
Studies found that a single large dose raised testosterone variably and that daily lower doses had no effect on strength, muscle size or body fat. The US classed it as an anabolic steroid in 2004.
How it works: Androstenedione is a precursor in the pathway to testosterone and estrogens. Oral doses may be converted to testosterone in some people, and estradiol also rose in studies.
Risks and caveats: The FDA banned its sale in 2004, and a 2004 US law added it to controlled-substance schedules, effective 2005. It is banned by the WADA, the Olympics and major sports leagues. Reported effects in women included masculinization and menstrual disturbance.
deepLead:
Prohormones are precursor compounds converted in the body to active hormones. In bodybuilding supplement culture the term covers androstenedione (4-AD, or andro) and related compounds such as 1-androstenedione, which were sold over the counter as testosterone boosters before regulatory action.
Androstenedione was introduced to the North American supplement market with credit given to Patrick Arnold, and was used widely in Major League Baseball during the 1990s, including by Mark McGwire. The International Olympic Committee banned it in 1997. The FDA banned its sale on April 11, 2004, and the Anabolic Steroid Control Act of 2004, effective January 20, 2005, classed androstenedione and other prohormones under the Controlled Substances Act.

name: Casein protein

angle.text: Users take casein before bed to supply amino acids slowly overnight and support muscle gain. Its digestion profile is well documented, while the added visible muscle versus other protein is untested.

summary: Slow-digesting milk protein taken before bed; digestion is well documented, appearance benefit untested.
note: Unsuitable for milk-protein allergy.
currentQuick:
Casein is the main protein in milk and is sold as a powder. It digests slowly, which is why bodybuilders and forum users take it before bed.
It is a food-grade protein, not a drug. Evidence relates to muscle protein, not to facial or aesthetic changes.
How it works: In the stomach casein forms a gel and releases amino acids over several hours, compared with the faster absorption of whey.
Risks and caveats: Main concern is milk-protein allergy or intolerance. Otherwise it is a common food ingredient sold without prescription.
deepLead:
Casein is the main protein family in milk, making up roughly 80% of cow's milk protein, and is sold as a powdered supplement (commonly micellar casein or calcium caseinate) in the bodybuilding and fitness market . In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed mainly as a slow-digesting protein taken before bed to support muscle mass.
The reasoning behind the use is that casein forms a gel in the stomach and releases amino acids gradually over several hours, in contrast to whey, which is absorbed faster . Proponents therefore pair whey after training with casein at other times, particularly overnight.
Published human work on casein as a muscle supplement consists largely of small exercise trials; a registered 2025 trial compared pre-sleep and post-exercise casein in 24 participants . Casein is a common food allergen in a small share of children, and people with milk protein allergy or intolerance avoid it .

name: Laxogenin

angle.text: Sold in bodybuilding supplements as a plant steroid that builds muscle without drugs. Research is limited to lab and plant studies, with no human trials of the muscle claim.

summary: Plant steroid-like saponin sold for muscle; research is lab and plant work only, no human trials.
note: No human safety or efficacy data found.
currentQuick:
Laxogenin is a compound from plants like Allium chinense, marketed to bodybuilders as a natural anabolic.
Its published research is chemistry, cell and plant work. No human trial was found.
How it works: No human mechanism for muscle growth has been published. Lab work covers cell assays and plant growth regulation.
Risks and caveats: No human safety data were found. Supplement contents can vary, and analytical studies have been needed to identify spirostanes in products.
deepLead:
Laxogenin is a plant-derived steroidal sapogenin (3-beta-hydroxy-5-alpha-spirostan-6-one) first characterised from plants such as Allium chinense (the 'Xiebai' bulb of Chinese medicine) and Smilax sieboldii . It is sold in bodybuilding supplements under claims of muscle-building, often described as a 'plant steroid'.
Published literature on laxogenin consists of phytochemistry, cell-culture and plant-growth work. One study of antitumour-promoting activity in cell assays and one analytical study identifying spirostanes in bodybuilding supplements exist . No published human trial of laxogenin for muscle or appearance was found.

name: Tribulus terrestris

angle.text: Taken as an herbal testosterone booster in hopes of more muscle and drive. Controlled studies have not consistently shown a hormone effect, so the appearance link rests mostly on supplement marketing.

summary: Herbal 'testosterone booster' sold since the 1980s; controlled studies have not consistently shown a hormone effect.
note: NCCIH says safety not proven; athlete bodies discourage use.
currentQuick:
Tribulus is a spiny plant whose extracts are sold as testosterone and libido supplements.
Controlled human studies have not consistently shown a testosterone effect, and no high-quality trial supports strength gains.
How it works: Marketing points to steroidal saponins such as protodioscin; supporting evidence is mainly from rodent and primate studies.
Risks and caveats: Safety in humans has not been proven according to the NCCIH. Sheep suffer photodermatitis from the plant; confirmed human reactions are not documented.
deepLead:
Tribulus terrestris (puncture vine, goathead) is a spiny annual plant of the caltrop family, native to warm regions of Eurasia and Africa and invasive elsewhere . Its fruit and leaf extracts have been used in traditional Chinese and Ayurvedic medicine and have been sold since the 1980s as a supplement intended to raise testosterone for bodybuilding or sexual function .
Published controlled studies have not consistently shown a testosterone effect in humans, and the US National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health states it has not been proven safe, according to Wikipedia . The Australian Institute of Sport discourages athlete use .

name: Caffeine pre-workout

angle.text: Users take stimulant pre-workouts to train with more intensity and focus in pursuit of more muscle. Caffeine has the best support for improving performance; the effect on physique itself is not directly studied.

summary: Stimulant-based training powders; caffeine is the best-supported ingredient and the rest is mixed.
note: High stimulant loads can raise blood pressure and cause anxiety and insomnia.
currentQuick:
Pre-workouts are powders taken before the gym, built around caffeine plus ingredients such as creatine, beta-alanine and citrulline.
Caffeine has well-documented effects on exercise performance. Evidence for other ingredients is mixed, and the benefit relates to training, not facial or body aesthetics directly.
How it works: Caffeine blocks adenosine receptors, raising alertness and lowering perceived effort.
Risks and caveats: Anxiety, insomnia and raised blood pressure are documented; ingredient accuracy varies and banned stimulants (ephedrine, DMAA) have appeared in the category.
deepLead:
Pre-workout supplements are multi-ingredient powders, capsules or drinks taken before training to increase energy, focus and endurance; caffeine is their near-universal base, found in 86% of bestselling products in one analysis . Other typical ingredients include creatine, beta-alanine, citrulline, amino acids and nitrates .
Caffeine itself is described as a proven ergogenic aid at moderate doses, with documented improvements in sprint, endurance and strength outcomes . Evidence for the other blend ingredients is mixed, and doses in commercial products are often below those studied . Regulators have acted against some stimulants sold in the category, such as ephedrine (2004) and DMAA (2012) .

name: Essential amino acids (EAAs)

chain: Muscle kept or built while dieting
angle.text: Fitness users take EAA powder as an alternative to protein powder to support muscle building, especially while cutting. EAAs stimulate muscle protein synthesis, and the aesthetic payoff versus ordinary protein is unstudied.

summary: The nine dietary amino acids as a powder; they drive muscle protein synthesis, but aesthetic payoff versus ordinary protein is unstudied.
note: No typical-dose human safety data in sources reviewed.
currentQuick:
EAAs are the nine amino acids the body must get from food, sold as a powder.
They stimulate muscle protein synthesis, with leucine central. Evidence compared with ordinary protein for physique is limited.
How it works: Amino acids, particularly leucine, signal through mTOR to switch on muscle protein synthesis.
Risks and caveats: Human safety data at typical supplement doses were not found; mouse BCAA work raises open metabolic questions.
deepLead:
Essential amino acids (EAAs) are nine amino acids that humans cannot synthesise fast enough to meet needs and must obtain from food: histidine, isoleucine, leucine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan and valine . EAA supplements sell these as a free-form powder, positioned in fitness communities as an alternative to protein powder for muscle building, especially during dieting.
Research shows EAAs stimulate muscle protein synthesis, and a lot of this work centres on leucine content in older adults . Studies on healthy young lifters taking EAA powders versus whole protein for visible physique outcomes are limited in the sources reviewed.

name: Epicatechin

angle.text: Promoted to lifters as a myostatin inhibitor that could allow extra muscle growth. Evidence is limited to small pilots in muscular dystrophy patients, not lifters.

summary: Cocoa/tea flavanol marketed as a myostatin inhibitor; evidence is small muscular-dystrophy pilots, not lifters.
note: Muscle data come from small patient pilots.
currentQuick:
Epicatechin is a polyphenol in cocoa and tea, sold as a muscle supplement.
The myostatin story rests on a seven-man Becker muscular dystrophy pilot. Controlled trials in healthy lifters were not found.
How it works: Proponents say it lowers myostatin and raises follistatin; evidence is biopsy markers in a small patient pilot and animal work.
Risks and caveats: Acute toxicity is low in rodents; mild GI effects are reported at higher catechin intakes. Other catechins (green tea extract) have liver safety concerns.
deepLead:
(-)-Epicatechin is a flavan-3-ol, a type of plant polyphenol found in cocoa, green tea, apples and berries . As a supplement it is promoted for muscle growth on the theory that it lowers myostatin and raises follistatin.
That theory comes mainly from a small open-label pilot in seven men with Becker muscular dystrophy, in which muscle biopsies showed higher follistatin and lower myostatin after eight weeks . Controlled trials in healthy lifters were not found; the Wikipedia catechin article does not discuss muscle effects at all . Other human work examines blood vessel function, and epicatechin trials in muscular dystrophy are small .

name: Phosphatidic acid

angle.text: Taken before training because it signals to mTOR, the pathway that drives muscle growth, in hopes of added muscle. Direct human evidence for extra muscle is small and thin.

summary: A membrane lipid sold as a pre-workout supplement because it signals to mTOR in cells; direct human evidence for added muscle is small and thin.
note: Cell-biology findings on mTOR are well established; evidence that oral supplements add muscle in people rests on very few small trials.
currentQuick:
Phosphatidic acid (PA) is a naturally occurring phospholipid found in every cell membrane. It is also sold as an over-the-counter supplement marketed to people who lift weights, on the premise that it activates the mTOR growth pathway.
The cell-biology link between PA and mTOR is well documented. Whether swallowing PA raises PA levels in muscle, and whether that produces extra muscle in people, has been tested in only a few small trials, and the ClinicalTrials.gov registrations for such studies are small.
How it works: In cell experiments, PA binds a domain of the mTOR protein and is needed for mitogen-driven activation of mTOR signaling, which regulates protein synthesis and cell growth [1][2]. Supplement proponents extrapolate from this to muscle growth after resistance training. Other work shows mTORC1 controls the location of lipin 1, an enzyme that processes PA [3].
Risks and caveats: PA is sold as a dietary supplement in the US, where supplements are regulated as foods and manufacturers are responsible for confirming safety [4]. Published safety data for supplemental PA in healthy lifters are limited. Because it is a general cell-signaling lipid, its role in other tissues has been studied mainly in laboratory research.
deepLead:
Phosphatidic acid (PA) is the simplest glycerophospholipid: a glycerol backbone carrying two fatty acid chains and a phosphate group. It is a precursor for other membrane lipids and also acts as a signaling molecule inside cells .
In looksmaxxing and bodybuilding communities PA is discussed as an over-the-counter, mTOR-activating supplement taken around resistance training with the aim of adding muscle size and strength. The marketing rationale draws on a 2001 Science paper reporting that PA binds mTOR and is required for its activation in cultured cells .
The cell-level mechanism is well characterised, but evidence that oral PA supplements increase muscle in humans is limited to a small number of short trials, and published independent replication is sparse.

name: Mass gainer powders

angle.text: Hard gainers use these calorie-dense shakes to eat enough to gain size and muscle. They reliably add calories, and the evidence concerns overall energy intake rather than the powder itself.

summary: Calorie-dense carb-and-protein shake powders for lifters who struggle to eat enough; they add calories, and the evidence is about overall energy intake rather than the powder itself.
note: Some products have been linked to contamination with undeclared steroids; one case report links a steroid-containing mass gainer to pancreatitis.
currentQuick:
A mass gainer is a powdered supplement mixed into a shake that delivers a large number of calories per serving, usually from carbohydrate, protein and fat. It is aimed at people trying to gain body weight and muscle who find it hard to eat enough food.
According to Grokipedia, typical servings supply 500 to 1,500 calories with a protein-to-carbohydrate ratio of around 1:2 or more [1]. Looksmaxxing forum users disagree about whether they are useful or whole food is preferable [2].
How it works: The mechanism is a caloric surplus: eating more energy than is used is needed to gain weight, and resistance training directs part of the gain toward muscle. A powder is a convenient, energy-dense way to add calories, often built on whey and maltodextrin [1]. A registered overfeeding-plus-resistance-training trial has examined body composition changes under surplus feeding, but results are not described in the registration [3].
Risks and caveats: Dietary supplements in the US are regulated as foods and manufacturers confirm product safety themselves [4]. A review of FDA data found muscle-building products among those contaminated with undeclared anabolic steroids [4], and a 2025 case report describes pancreatitis with panniculitis in a patient who took a weight-gain supplement thought to contain anabolic steroids [5]. Users also report digestive complaints and acne in forums [2].
deepLead:
A mass gainer, or weight gainer, is a high-calorie powder supplement designed to help people gain weight and muscle by supplying a large amount of energy, mostly from carbohydrate with moderate protein and some fat, in a drinkable form .
Mass gainers are discussed in bodybuilding and looksmaxxing communities by "hardgainers" and by people bulking. Some lifters regard them as a convenient way to hit calorie targets; others in the same forums argue that whole foods or plain protein are preferable .
Evidence specific to mass gainers as a product category is limited. The underlying principle, that weight gain requires a caloric surplus, is general nutrition; published case reports describe harms from products adulterated with steroids .
